title: Northwest Airlines 2
summary: A Lockheed Super Electra en route from Seattle to Chicago diverted north to avoid a dust storm over Bozeman Pass. As the aircraft passed over the Bridger Mountain range at approximately 8500 feet elevation, ground witnesses reported it immediately dropped, went into a stall, glided briefly, then spun into the ground. The wreckage burst into flames and all ten occupants were killed.
probable_cause: Unknown; aircraft encountered dust storm requiring diversion north over mountainous terrain.

factors.evidence: Dust storm over Bozeman Pass forced aircraft to divert north over Bridger Mountains
Ground witnesses reported aircraft went into a stall as it passed over Bridger Mountain range
Ground witnesses reported aircraft went into stall, glided for short time, then spun into ground
Aircraft crashed on snow-covered peak high in Bridger Mountains

title: 1938 Yosemite TWA crash
summary: A Douglas DC-2 encountered severe weather during descent from San Francisco to Winslow and diverted toward Fresno. The pilot experienced ice formation on wings and confusion about position relative to the Fresno Radio Range station. A sharp increase in wind velocity combined with the pilot's positional confusion resulted in flight over mountainous terrain in Yosemite National Park, ending in a crash.
probable_cause: A change in wind direction and a sharp increase in velocity unknown to the pilot, together with pilot confusion as to position with reference to the Fresno Radio Range station, which combined to bring about flight over mountainous terrain, ending in a crash.

factors.evidence: the flight encountered a building weather front that developed into the most severe storm on the West Coast in 64 years
Captain Graves noticed ice forming on the wings
a change in wind direction and a sharp increase in velocity, unknown to the pilot
pilot's confusion as to his position with reference to the Fresno Radio Range station
aircraft subsequently crashed on a mountain in Yosemite National Park

events.text: Flight 8 was flying from San Francisco to Winslow, which was a hub connecting TWA's transcontinental route.
Two hours after takeoff, the flight encountered a building weather front that developed into the most severe storm on the West Coast in 64 years.
Captain Graves noticed ice forming on the wings and advised air traffic controllers, who ordered him to divert to Los Angeles due to the deteriorating weather conditions.
At 9:28 PM, he requested a weather update; this was his last transmission received by air traffic control and the aircraft subsequently crashed on a mountain in Yosemite National Park.

title: Kweilin Incident
summary: A Douglas DC-2 airliner named Kweilin operated by China National Aviation Corporation was shot down by eight Japanese pontoon-fitted aircraft on 24 August 1938 while flying from Hong Kong to Chengdu. The aircraft was unarmed and pilot Hugh Leslie Woods made a perfect water landing in a river when attacked. The Japanese continued strafing the aircraft for about an hour, riddling it with bullets until it sank. Fifteen of 18 aboard died including prominent Chinese bankers.
probable_cause: The aircraft was attacked by Japanese military aircraft; it was speculated the attack intended to assassinate Chinese politician Sun Fo but he had taken an earlier flight.

factors.evidence: The aircraft was shot down by Japanese aircraft in what the pilot believed to be an attacking formation.
Pilot made a perfect water landing in a river when attacked by Japanese planes.
Three survivors including pilot Woods, radio operator Joe Loh and wounded passenger Lou Zhaonian survived the ditching and aftermath.
Japanese aircraft continued strafing the floating aircraft with machine gun fire for about an hour, destroying it.

events.text: DC-2 Kweilin departed Hong Kong at 8:04am with 14 passengers, steward, radio operator Joe Loh, copilot Lieu Chung-chuan, and American pilot Hugh Leslie Woods.
Soon after entering Chinese airspace, Woods spotted eight Japanese pontoon-fitted planes in what he believed to be an attacking formation.
Woods took evasive maneuvers by circling into a cloud bank and was fired upon by the Japanese planes, their intentions made clear.
Woods put the aircraft into a fast dive to find a place to make an emergency landing, then made a perfect water landing in a river.
Japanese aircraft began to strafe the floating aircraft with machine gun fire and continued attacks for about an hour, riddling it with bullets.
Among the survivors were Woods, the radio operator Joe Loh and a wounded passenger, Lou Zhaonian; the dead included two women, a five-year-old boy and a baby.

title: 1938 Japan mid-air collision
operator: Nippon Flying School / Japan Air Transport
summary: An Imperial Japanese Army Air Force Mitsubishi Ka 1 military trainer collided in midair with a Japan Air Transport Fokker Super Universal airliner over Tokyo's Ōmori district. Both aircraft were destroyed, killing five aircrews. The impact caused a fire that burned the wreckage on the ground, and a fuel tank explosion minutes later killed or injured a large crowd of onlookers gathered at the site.

title: 1938 Kyeema crash
summary: Douglas DC-2 crashed into Mount Dandenong near Melbourne on approach in heavy fog. Flight crew mistakenly identified Sunbury as Daylesford through a gap in clouds, believing they were 30 km behind their actual location. Unable to see through fog after overrunning Essendon, the aircraft struck the western slopes of the mountain, killing all 18 on board.
probable_cause: Navigation error leading to controlled flight into terrain in low visibility conditions.

factors.evidence: Heavy fog and cloud layer extending from 1500 ft near Melbourne
Flight crew mistakenly identified Sunbury as Daylesford, believing they were 30 km behind actual location
Pilots becoming unsure of their position and did not cross-reference ground speed with previous landmarks
Aircraft crashed into western slopes of Mount Dandenong

events.text: Flight took off from Adelaide and climbed toward Melbourne
Aircraft entered area around Melbourne with heavy cloud layer extending from 1500 ft, making landmark navigation difficult
Flight crew mistakenly identified Sunbury as Daylesford through gap in clouds, believing they were 30 km behind where they actually were on their flight plan
Aircraft overshot Essendon due to misidentification of position and was unable to see through heavy fog
